988.short: The national three-digit number for a mental health or suicide crisis, by call, text or chat, at any hour.

admh.short: The state agency responsible for public mental health, substance use and developmental disability services in Alabama.

state-mental-health-authority.short: The agency in each state that is accountable for the public mental health system and reports on it to the federal government. In Alabama it is ADMH.

admh-commissioner.short: The head of the Alabama Department of Mental Health, appointed by the Governor.

admh-board-of-trustees.short: The sixteen-member board, chaired by the Governor, that oversees the Department of Mental Health and meets quarterly.

admh-strategic-plan.term: ADMH Strategic Plan 2025–2028 (and the goal codes A1 to E3)
admh-strategic-plan.short: The Department's plan, built on five priorities. The codes such as A1 or B4 are this report's labels for goals under each priority.

five-year-plan.short: Targets the Commissioner presented to legislators in February 2025: more civil beds, more mobile crisis teams, more crisis centers.

legislative-services-agency.term: Legislative Services Agency (LSA) and its comparison sheets
legislative-services-agency.short: The Legislature's staff agency. Its line-by-line budget comparison sheets are this report's source for what was appropriated.

aces.term: Alabama Commission on the Evaluation of Services (ACES)
aces.short: A state commission, created in 2019, that evaluates whether state programs work and advises the Legislature and the Governor.

state-mental-health-planning-council.short: A council every state must keep as a condition of the federal mental health block grant, with people who use services among its members.

sb101-consent-age.term: SB101 (Act 2025-455): age of consent for treatment
sb101-consent-age.short: A 2025 Alabama law raising from 14 to 16 the age at which a minor can consent alone to medical and mental health treatment.

parental-opt-in.term: Parental opt-in consent for school mental health services (Act 2022-442)
parental-opt-in.short: Since 2022 Alabama schools need a parent's written permission before a student receives ongoing mental health services.

sb236-regional-boards.term: SB236 (Act 2025-366): sheriffs and probate judges on regional boards
sb236-regional-boards.short: A 2025 law that puts a sheriff and a probate judge on the executive committee of larger regional mental health boards.

accountability-courts.short: Alabama's new name for drug courts, which since October 2025 may also take defendants with mental illness and veterans.

specialty-courts.term: Specialty courts (mental health, veterans and drug courts)
specialty-courts.short: Court dockets that put eligible defendants under supervised treatment in place of ordinary prosecution or jail.

houston-hunter-act.short: A 2025 Alabama law letting a person voluntarily leave firearms with a licensed dealer for a time, as a suicide-prevention measure.

lethal-means.short: The method a person might use to end their life. Putting time and distance between a person in crisis and a gun or drugs lowers risk.

hb487.short: The 2026 bill that appropriated $43.1 million of opioid-settlement money across agencies, most of it to ADMH.

federal-budget-law-2025.short: The federal budget reconciliation law of July 2025, which changed Medicaid financing rules and tightened SNAP work requirements.

civil-commitment.short: A court order requiring a person with mental illness to accept treatment because they pose a serious danger. It is not a criminal matter.

probate-court.short: The county court that, in Alabama, hears petitions for civil commitment. Each county has a probate judge.

clear-and-convincing-evidence.short: A standard of proof: stronger than "more likely than not", weaker than "beyond a reasonable doubt". Alabama requires it for commitment.

least-restrictive-alternative.short: The rule that a court must choose the form of treatment that limits a person's liberty no more than is needed.

outpatient-commitment.short: A court order to follow a treatment plan while living in the community rather than in a hospital.

involuntary-beds.short: Psychiatric beds available for people under a civil-commitment order. ADMH counted 771 in January 2026.

beds-per-100000.short: A way of comparing psychiatric bed supply with population. ADMH plans against a benchmark of 30 beds per 100,000 residents.

forensic.short: Mental health services ordered by criminal courts: evaluating whether a defendant can stand trial and treating those who cannot.

competency-evaluation.short: An examination, ordered by a criminal court, of whether a defendant understands the proceedings well enough to be tried.

competency-restoration.short: Treatment meant to make a defendant found incompetent able to stand trial. Until it happens the criminal case is on hold.

jail-based-restoration.short: Restoration treatment delivered inside a county jail, in person or by video, instead of waiting for a state hospital bed.

forensic-waitlist.short: The number of people held in county jails while waiting for a court-ordered competency evaluation or a restoration bed.

forensic-navigators.short: Department staff who work the forensic waitlist, identifying people who may be better served outside the forensic system.

hunter-consent-decree.term: Hunter v. Boswell (the Hunter consent decree)
hunter-consent-decree.short: A federal court settlement, in force since 2018, that limits how long people may wait in Alabama jails for competency services.

braggs.term: Braggs v. Commissioner (the prison mental health case)
braggs.short: A federal class action in which a court found in 2017 that mental health care in Alabama's prisons was unconstitutional.

wyatt-v-stickney.short: The 1971 Alabama case that established a constitutional right to adequate treatment for people confined in state psychiatric hospitals.

consent-decree.short: A settlement of a lawsuit that a court approves and then enforces as its own order.

eighth-amendment.short: The part of the U.S. Constitution that bans cruel and unusual punishments. Courts read it to require adequate health care in prisons.

general-fund.short: One of Alabama's two main state budgets. It pays for most non-education agencies, including mental health, Medicaid and prisons.

education-trust-fund.short: Alabama's separate state budget for education. A small part of it reaches ADMH, mostly for services tied to schools and children.

special-mental-health-fund.short: A state fund fed by earmarked taxes that may be spent only on mental health. It supplied about a sixth of ADMH's revenue in FY2025.

appropriation.short: The Legislature's legal permission for an agency to spend a set amount of public money in a given year.

appropriation-conditions.short: Strings the Legislature attaches to money. In FY2027 part of ADMH's crisis funding is held back until the Department reports on results.

fiscal-year.short: A budget year. Alabama's runs from 1 October to 30 September and is named for the year in which it ends.

block-grant.term: Mental Health Block Grant (federal block grants)
block-grant.short: Federal money given to each state by formula for community mental health services, with planning and reporting duties attached.

opioid-settlement-funds.short: Money paid to the state under legal settlements with opioid makers and distributors, appropriated by the Legislature for treatment and prevention.

rural-health-transformation.short: A federally funded grant program, run in Alabama by ADECA, that began awarding money to rural health providers in August 2026.

spending-per-resident.term: State mental health agency spending per resident
spending-per-resident.short: What a state's mental health agency spends in a year divided by the state's population, used to compare states.

medicaid.short: The public health insurance program for low-income people, paid for jointly by the federal government and the state.

fmap.short: The share of Medicaid costs the federal government pays. Poorer states get a higher share; Alabama's is about 73 percent.

enhanced-match.short: A federal share of Medicaid costs higher than a state's usual rate, offered to encourage a particular service or policy.

medicaid-expansion.short: The option, under the Affordable Care Act, for a state to cover low-income adults whatever their family or health status. Alabama has not taken it.

coverage-gap.short: Adults who earn too much for Alabama's Medicaid but too little to qualify for subsidized marketplace insurance.

federal-poverty-level.short: An income figure the federal government sets each year, by family size, and uses to decide who qualifies for programs.

state-plan-amendment.term: Medicaid state plan and state plan amendment (SPA)
state-plan-amendment.short: The state plan is Alabama's standing agreement with the federal government on how it runs Medicaid. An amendment changes it.

section-1115-waiver.short: Federal permission for a state to test a Medicaid approach that the ordinary rules would not allow, for a limited period.

medicaid-reentry-waiver.short: A Section 1115 waiver that lets Medicaid pay for some health services shortly before a person leaves jail or prison.

medicaid-suspension.short: Alabama pauses, and does not cancel, a person's Medicaid eligibility while they are in prison or jail.

institution-for-mental-disease.short: Medicaid's term for a psychiatric or substance use facility with more than 16 beds. Medicaid usually will not pay for adults' stays in one.

fee-for-service.short: Payment by the item: the provider bills a set fee for each visit or procedure. More services mean more payment.

managed-care.short: An arrangement in which a state pays health plans a fixed amount per member and the plans arrange and pay for care.

alabama-coordinated-health-network.short: Alabama Medicaid's care-coordination program, organized in seven regions. It coordinates care but does not pay for it as a health plan would.

medicaid-rehabilitative-services.short: The Medicaid benefit that pays for community mental health and substance use treatment delivered by ADMH-certified providers.

commercial-insurance.short: Private health insurance, most often obtained through a job. Half of Alabamians are covered this way.

marketplace.short: The federal exchange (HealthCare.gov) where people without job-based coverage buy insurance, often with a subsidy tied to income.

provider-tax.short: A tax a state charges hospitals or other providers and uses to pay its own share of Medicaid, drawing federal match in return.

mental-health-parity.short: The legal rule that an insurance plan may not limit mental health benefits more tightly than medical and surgical benefits.

postpartum-coverage.short: Medicaid coverage that continues for a year after a birth instead of ending after 60 days.

ccbhc.short: A clinic certified to provide nine required mental health and substance use services and paid a set daily rate by Medicaid.

prospective-payment.term: Prospective payment (the CCBHC daily rate, PPS-1)
prospective-payment.short: A payment set in advance. A CCBHC gets one fixed amount for each day it gives a Medicaid enrollee a qualifying service, whatever the service.

cost-report.short: A clinic's formal statement of what it costs to operate, used to set its CCBHC daily rate.

section-223-demonstration.short: The federal program under which selected states pay CCBHCs through Medicaid at a prospective rate. Alabama joined in June 2024.

designated-collaborating-organization.short: A separate provider that a CCBHC contracts with to deliver one of its required services.

community-mental-health-center.short: One of the 19 regional organizations that deliver most public outpatient mental health care in Alabama under contract with ADMH.

regional-310-board.term: Regional mental health authority board (310 board)
regional-310-board.short: The public corporation that governs a community mental health center. The nickname comes from Act 310 of 1967, the law that allows them.

admh-certification.short: The Department's approval that a community provider meets its standards. Without it a provider cannot bill Medicaid for these services.

crisis-system.term: Crisis system: someone to contact, someone to respond, a safe place for help
crisis-system.short: The national model for mental health crisis care, built from three parts: a line to call, a team that comes out, and a place to go.

in-state-answer-rate.short: The share of 988 calls from Alabama that are answered by a counselor in Alabama instead of rolling over to a national backup center.

georouting.short: Sending a 988 call or text to the crisis center nearest the person's rough location, not the one matching the phone's area code.

veterans-crisis-line.short: The crisis line for veterans and service members, reached by dialing 988 and pressing 1.

mobile-crisis.short: Clinicians who travel to a person in crisis, at home or elsewhere in the community, in place of police or an ambulance.

crisis-diversion-center.short: A walk-in center, open at all hours, where a person in mental health crisis can be assessed and stabilized instead of going to an emergency room or jail.

observation-beds.short: Short-stay beds in a crisis center where a person is watched and treated for hours or a few days, not admitted to a hospital.

crisis-residential.short: A small staffed residence where a person in crisis can stay for a short period as an alternative to a hospital ward.

pediatric-crisis-unit.short: A crisis center for young people. Alabama has one, WellStone's 24-bed unit in Huntsville for ages 12 to 18.

rural-crisis-care.short: State-funded programs that bring crisis response to rural counties far from any of the six crisis centers.

diversion.short: Steering a person away from a costlier or more harmful setting, such as jail or an emergency room, and into care or a community program.

co-responder.short: A police unit in which a mental health clinician rides with or joins an officer on calls involving a person in crisis.

ed-boarding.short: Holding a psychiatric patient in an emergency room, sometimes for days, because no inpatient bed or placement is available.

catchment.short: The set of counties a facility is assigned to serve. It shows who is responsible for an area, not how far people must travel.

utilization.short: How much of a facility's capacity is in use, usually the share of available beds that are filled over a period.

bed-day.short: One bed occupied for one day. Cost per bed-day divides a facility's spending by the number of bed-days it delivered.

service-continuum.short: The full range of mental health services arranged by intensity, from promotion and prevention through treatment and crisis care to recovery supports.

beyond-beds.short: A 2017 national policy paper arguing that psychiatric hospital beds work only as one part of a complete range of services.

promotion-and-prevention.short: The earliest part of the continuum: building mental well-being in everyone and acting before a disorder develops.

outpatient.short: Treatment a person attends by appointment while living at home: therapy, psychiatric visits, medication management.

step-down.short: A less intensive setting a person moves to after a hospital or crisis stay, such as a staffed residence, before living independently.

recovery-supports.short: The services that help a person keep a home, a job and relationships once the acute illness is treated.

residential-services.short: Places to live with staff support, in grades from closely supervised homes to semi-independent apartments, funded through community contracts.

supported-housing.short: An ordinary home paired with visiting support services, so that a person with serious mental illness can live in the community.

supported-employment.short: Help finding and keeping an ordinary paid job, with a specialist who supports both the worker and the employer.

individual-placement-and-support.short: The evidence-based model of supported employment for people with serious mental illness: a quick job search, then lasting support.

assertive-community-treatment.short: A team of clinicians that brings intensive treatment to people with serious mental illness where they live, instead of waiting for clinic visits.

case-management.short: Help from a named worker who links a person to treatment, benefits and housing, and keeps the pieces connected.

first-episode-psychosis.term: First-episode psychosis programs (coordinated specialty care; NOVA)
first-episode-psychosis.short: Team-based early treatment for young people having a first psychotic episode. Alabama's three programs use the name NOVA.

peer-support-specialist.short: A person in recovery from mental illness or addiction who is trained and certified to support others going through the same.

peer-run-organization.short: An organization led and staffed by people who have themselves lived with mental illness or addiction.

integrated-care.short: Mental health care delivered inside primary care, with the family doctor and a mental health clinician working as one team.

fqhc.short: A federally funded community clinic that provides primary care to anyone, with fees scaled to income.

serious-mental-illness.short: A mental disorder in an adult that seriously limits daily life, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or severe depression.

serious-emotional-disturbance.short: The children's counterpart of serious mental illness: a diagnosable disorder in someone under 18 that seriously limits life at home, at school or with others.

developmental-disabilities.short: Lifelong conditions that begin in childhood and affect learning and daily living, such as intellectual disability and autism.

substance-use-disorder.short: The clinical term for addiction: continued use of alcohol or drugs despite serious harm. Opioid use disorder is one kind.

medication-assisted-treatment.short: Treating opioid addiction with a prescribed medicine, such as buprenorphine or methadone, usually alongside counseling.

naloxone.short: A medicine that reverses an opioid overdose within minutes, often given as a nasal spray.

detoxification.short: Medically supervised withdrawal from alcohol or drugs. It is the first step of treatment, not the whole of it.

state-hospital.short: A psychiatric hospital owned and run by the state. Alabama has three, operated by ADMH.

taylor-hardin.short: The state's forensic psychiatric hospital, in Tuscaloosa, for people sent by the criminal courts.

telehealth.short: Care delivered at a distance by video or telephone. Audio-only means an ordinary phone call with no video.

telehealth-parity.short: Paying a provider the same for a visit by video or phone as for the same visit in person.

bead.short: The federal grant program paying to bring high-speed internet to homes and businesses that have none.

one-health-record.term: One Health Record (Alabama's health information exchange)
one-health-record.short: Alabama's network for sharing patient records electronically between hospitals, clinics and other providers.

tefca-qhin.short: TEFCA is the federal framework for sharing health records nationwide. A QHIN is one of the approved networks that carry the traffic.

42-cfr-part-2.short: The federal rule that gives substance use treatment records stricter confidentiality protection than other health records.

acsis.short: ADMH's reporting system for mental illness and CCBHC providers: clients, episodes of care, staff and billing.

asais.short: ADMH's reporting and billing system for substance use treatment providers.

ccbhc-outcomes-platform.short: The software ADMH has bought so that CCBHCs can report the outcome measures the federal demonstration requires.

hpsa.short: A place, population or facility the federal government has designated as having too few health care providers.

need-met.short: In federal shortage data, the share of the psychiatrists a shortage area would need that it actually has.

workforce-availability.short: Residents per mental health provider. Mental Health America ranks Alabama last on it, at 740 residents for each provider.

national-health-service-corps.short: A federal program that repays clinicians' student loans in return for working in a shortage area.

licensure-compact.short: An agreement among states that lets a clinician licensed in one member state practice in the others, in person or by telehealth.

psypact.short: The compact that lets psychologists practice by telehealth, and for short periods in person, across member states.

counseling-compact.short: The compact for licensed professional counselors. Alabama is a member, but it is not yet working in Alabama.

nurse-licensure-compact.short: The compact under which a nurse holds one multistate licence valid in all member states.

social-work-compact.short: The compact for social workers. Alabama joined in 2024; multistate licences are not yet being issued.

direct-support-professional.short: A front-line worker who helps people with developmental disabilities with daily living, at home or in a residence.

psychiatry-residency.short: The years of supervised hospital training a doctor completes after medical school to become a psychiatrist; a fellowship adds a subspecialty.

faith-based-support-specialist.short: A faith leader certified, after a short training, to recognize addiction and connect people to treatment.

mental-health-first-aid.short: An eight-hour course that teaches members of the public to recognize and respond to someone developing a mental health problem or in crisis.

uniform-reporting-system.short: The standard set of tables each state mental health agency files with the federal government every year, published state by state.

penetration-rate.short: The number of people the public mental health system served in a year for every 1,000 residents of the state.

readmission-rate.short: The share of people discharged from a hospital who are admitted again within a set time, usually 30 or 180 days.

reporting-year.short: The twelve months a set of figures covers. For the federal tables it is October to September, not the calendar year.

consumer-survey.short: A survey of people who use public mental health services, asking about access, quality and results of their care.

rates-per-population.short: A count divided by population so that places of different size can be compared. The base (1,000 or 100,000) is a matter of convention.

rankings.short: A state's position in an ordered list. "Of 51" counts the states and the District of Columbia; "of 52" adds Puerto Rico.

all-ages-versus-adults.short: A label on a figure saying whether children are included. The same measure can differ noticeably between the two groups.

disaggregated-data.short: Figures broken down by group, such as race, county or age, so that differences hidden in a total can be seen.

provisional-figure.short: A preliminary count that is expected to change as late records arrive.

seven-day-follow-up.short: The share of people who see a mental health provider within seven days of leaving a psychiatric hospital.

mental-health-america.short: A national advocacy organization whose yearly report ranks the states on 17 measures of mental illness and access to care.

youth-risk-behavior-survey.short: A federal survey of high-school students on behaviors that affect health, including mental health and suicide.

kids-count.short: A collection of indicators of child well-being for Alabama and each county, compiled by VOICES for Alabama's Children.

maternal-mortality-review.short: A committee review of each death during or soon after pregnancy, to decide whether it was related to the pregnancy and preventable.

point-in-time-count.short: A count of everyone found homeless, in shelters and on the street, on a single night in January.

rural-definitions.short: This report uses two measures: counties classed as rural, and the share of people living in rural areas. They are not interchangeable.

sequential-intercept-model.short: A map of the points at which a person with mental illness can be turned from the criminal justice system toward treatment.

crisis-intervention-team.short: A program that trains police officers to respond to people in mental health crisis and links police with local mental health services.

apostc.term: Alabama Peace Officers' Standards and Training Commission (APOSTC)
apostc.short: The state body that sets training and certification standards for police officers.

stepping-up.short: A national initiative to reduce the number of people with mental illness in county jails, administered in Alabama by ADMH.

jail-screening.short: A short set of questions asked when a person is booked into jail, to identify mental illness or suicide risk early.

administrative-office-of-courts.short: The agency that manages Alabama's state court system on behalf of the Chief Justice.

adoc.short: The state agency that runs Alabama's prisons. Its mental health care is under federal court order.

pardons-and-paroles.term: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles
pardons-and-paroles.short: The state agency that supervises people on probation and parole and runs reentry programs.

parole-and-probation.short: Probation is supervision in the community in place of prison. Parole is supervised release after part of a prison sentence is served.

recidivism.short: Returning to crime or custody after release. The rate depends heavily on how "return" is defined and over how many years.

reentry.short: The return of a person from prison or jail to the community, and the services that support it.

reentry-task-force.term: Reentry Task Force and the Reentry Alabama plan
reentry-task-force.short: A state task force created in 2025 to carry out Alabama's plan for reducing reoffending among people leaving prison.

day-reporting-center.short: A facility where people on probation or parole report regularly for supervision, treatment and job help while living at home.

community-corrections.short: Locally run programs that supervise people convicted of crimes in the community as an alternative to prison.

who-building-blocks.short: The World Health Organization's six-part description of what any health system needs, which this report adapts into eight domains.

system-of-care.term: System of Care (children's mental health framework)
system-of-care.short: A national framework holding that services for children with serious mental health needs should be family-driven, community-based and coordinated across agencies.

social-determinants-of-health.short: The conditions of daily life, such as housing, income, schooling and transport, that shape health apart from medical care.

healthy-people-2030.short: The federal government's set of national health objectives for the decade to 2030.

trauma-informed-care.short: An approach that assumes many people seeking help have lived through trauma and organizes services so as not to repeat the harm.

clas-standards.short: National standards for health services that respect patients' culture and language, including interpreters at no cost.

hud-continuum-of-care.term: Continuum of Care (HUD homelessness planning body)
hud-continuum-of-care.short: A regional body, recognized by the federal housing department, that plans the local response to homelessness and sets priorities for federal funds.

emergency-solutions-grants.short: Federal money for emergency shelter, short-term rental help and related services, passed through the state to local agencies.

snap.short: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the federal food benefit once called food stamps.

ssi-and-ssdi.short: Two federal disability payments. SSDI is insurance earned through past work; SSI is a smaller payment for disabled people with very low income.

vocational-rehabilitation.short: The state program that helps people with disabilities prepare for and find work, run by the Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services.

office-of-child-and-family-services.term: ADMH Office of Child and Family Services
office-of-child-and-family-services.short: The ADMH office, created in October 2023, that brings the Department's programs for children and families under one roof.

school-based-mental-health.short: A program, begun in 2010, that places community mental health center clinicians in schools.

mental-health-services-coordinator.short: A school-district employee who links students to mental health services. State law requires every district to have one.

local-education-agency.short: The official term for a school district: a city or county school system.

alsde.short: The state agency that oversees Alabama's public schools.

paths.term: PATHS (Pediatric Access to Telemental Health Services)
paths.short: A consultation line through which primary-care doctors can get advice from child mental health specialists at Children's of Alabama.

infant-and-early-childhood-mental-health.short: Support for the emotional development of children from birth to about five, delivered mainly through the adults who care for them.

intensive-in-home-services.short: Frequent treatment delivered in the family home for a child at risk of being placed in a hospital or residential care.

wraparound.short: A way of planning care for a child with complex needs, in which one team builds a single plan around the family across all the agencies involved.

therapeutic-foster-care.short: Foster care with specially trained foster parents and clinical support, for children whose needs an ordinary foster home cannot meet.

out-of-home-care.short: The placement of a child, by the child-welfare agency, away from the family home: with relatives, foster parents or in a facility.

dhr.short: The state agency responsible for child protection and foster care, and for benefits such as SNAP.

dys.short: The state's juvenile justice agency. It holds young people committed by juvenile courts and funds local diversion programs.

home-visiting.short: Programs that send a trained visitor to the homes of pregnant women and families with young children to support parenting and health.

adece.term: Alabama Department of Early Childhood Education (ADECE)
adece.short: The state agency for pre-kindergarten and early-childhood programs, including home visiting.

childrens-policy-council.term: Alabama Children's Policy Council and the State Team
childrens-policy-council.short: Two bodies set up in state law to coordinate services for children across agencies. Neither is dedicated to mental health.

transitional-age.short: Young people moving from children's services to adult services, roughly from the late teens into the mid-twenties.

adeca.term: Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA)
adeca.short: The state agency that distributes many federal grants to local governments and nonprofits, from homelessness funds to broadband.

adph.short: The state public health agency. It is separate from ADMH and keeps the statistics on deaths, including suicides and overdoses.

va-facilities.term: VA medical centers, clinics and Vet Centers
va-facilities.short: The federal Department of Veterans Affairs' own health system: hospitals, outpatient clinics and community counseling centers for veterans.

cms.short: The federal agency that runs Medicare and oversees each state's Medicaid program.

samhsa.short: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, the federal agency for mental health and addiction services.

nami-alabama.short: The state organization of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, a membership group of people with mental illness and their families.

adap.short: A legal advocacy program for Alabamians with disabilities. It monitors the state's compliance with the Hunter consent decree.

voices-for-alabamas-children.short: A child advocacy organization that compiles the Alabama Kids Count data on child well-being.

asparc.term: Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition (ASPARC)
asparc.short: The nonprofit state coalition that trains people in suicide prevention and advocates for it.

alabama-arise.short: A statewide advocacy organization on poverty issues, and the coalition it leads to press for wider health coverage.

north-alabama-mental-health-coalition.short: A regional coalition, formed in 2015, of providers, law enforcement, officials, judges and advocates in North Alabama.

little-orange-fish.short: The organization that publishes this report.
